canonical_statement: The study objective was to evaluate the association between preexisting CKD severity and health outcomes after ICU admission.
The investigators conducted a population-based retrospective cohort study using linked health administrative databases held at ICES in Ontario, Canada.
The cohort accrual period was November 1, 2008, through February 28, 2021; only the first ICU admission for each individual was included.
Ontario residents aged 18 years or older admitted to an ICU during the accrual period were eligible.

population.label: Ontario adults admitted to an ICU

canonical_statement: Exclusions included prior kidney transplant, absence of a baseline eGFR, and ineligibility for Ontario Health Insurance Plan coverage.
Baseline kidney function was defined using the most recent outpatient serum creatinine measured 7 to 365 days before ICU admission, and eGFR was calculated with the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation.
CKD severity was categorized by baseline eGFR as ≥60, 45-59, 30-44, 15-29, <15 mL/min/1.73 m² without dialysis, or maintenance dialysis.

exposures.details: KDIGO eGFR categories plus maintenance dialysis

canonical_statement: The primary outcome was all-cause mortality during the ICU stay, during the hospitalization, and within 90 days after ICU admission.
Secondary outcomes were KRT during the ICU stay, KRT dependence at 90 days, and ICU and hospital lengths of stay.

Logistic regression estimated crude and adjusted associations of CKD stage with mortality outcomes and KRT initiation in the ICU; maintenance-dialysis patients were excluded from KRT initiation analyses.

Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models evaluated time to ICU and hospital discharge with in-hospital death treated as a competing event; a subdistribution HR below 1 corresponds to a lower discharge rate and longer stay.

Adjusted models included demographics, neighborhood income, major comorbidities, prior health care utilization, vasopressor and mechanical ventilation use, MODS with the renal component removed, sepsis, and severe sepsis including septic shock.

Additional analyses used Cox modeling for 90-day mortality, median outpatient creatinine to redefine baseline eGFR, imputation of eGFR 75 mL/min/1.73 m² for missing baseline creatinine, and albuminuria category as an exposure where available.
Of 848,202 Ontario residents admitted to an ICU during the accrual period, 531,090 met study eligibility criteria.
The eligible cohort had a mean age of 67 years (SD 15); 57% were men and 43% were women.
No CKD/eGFR ≥60 comprised 398,296 participants (75% of the cohort).
Stage 3a CKD/eGFR 45-59 comprised 63,825 participants (12% of the cohort).
Stage 3b CKD/eGFR 30-44 comprised 38,744 participants (7% of the cohort).
Stage 4 CKD/eGFR 15-29 comprised 17,207 participants (3% of the cohort).
Stage 5 CKD/eGFR <15, non-dialysis comprised 3,626 participants (1% of the cohort).
Maintenance dialysis comprised 9,392 participants (2% of the cohort).

The authors concluded that CKD was present in 25% of the ICU cohort and that greater CKD severity was associated with death, KRT dependence/ESKD, and longer ICU and hospital stays.
Mortality risk rose progressively through non–dialysis-dependent stage 5 CKD, while maintenance-dialysis patients had lower mortality risk than non-dialysis stage 5 and risk comparable to stage 4.
The authors stated that the findings may inform risk prognostication, goals-of-care discussions, resource allocation, and health policy for ICU patients with CKD.

The authors proposed several possible explanations for lower mortality among maintenance-dialysis patients than non-dialysis stage 5 patients, including tighter volume/metabolic control, ICU triage differences, survivor selection, and reversible dialysis-related admission problems; these were hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms.
Because the study was observational, it supports associations but not causation, and unobserved confounding may remain despite extensive adjustment.
Use of the most recent preadmission eGFR may misclassify chronic kidney function because of temporal variability, although a median-eGFR sensitivity analysis produced similar results.
The primary CKD definition used eGFR without albuminuria because most participants lacked recent albuminuria measurements; albuminuria was analyzed only in the 39.3% with available ACR.
AKI at ICU admission was not directly accounted for, leaving potential residual confounding related to acute kidney injury.
Administrative registry data lacked some clinical granularity, including the exact case-by-case reason for ICU admission.

Excluding patients without baseline outpatient creatinine may have introduced selection bias because excluded patients were generally younger and had fewer comorbidities; an imputed sensitivity analysis yielded similar findings.
